transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2025-05-09
- Start: 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~52 minutes
- Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jules Park (Redwood SE), Ralph Chen (CTO, Stellarium), Priya Nair (Lead ML), Diego Morales (SRE), Anika Bose (PM)

Summary:
Quick Optimize walkthrough focusing on how to tune batching and prefix/KV caching for Stellarium's high-concurrency conversational inference workloads. Reviewed three cost scenarios with KV hit rates, batching multipliers, and latency SLOs. Customer asked about hosted vs dedicated and VPC implications for throughput tests.

Topics:
- Cost model baseline assumptions (tokens, price per token, embeddings)
- Batching multipliers by concurrency and model size
- Prefix/KV cache hit-rate scenarios and prefetch strategies
- Latency budget tradeoffs (P95/P99) and routing fallbacks
- Sandbox load test plan and security artifacts

Action items (recap at end are separate): see metadata action_items.

Transcript:
[00:00:05] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick roll call?
[00:00:10] Ralph: Ralph here. Priya, Diego and Anika with me.
[00:00:13] Priya: Hi all.
[00:00:15] Jules: Jules from Redwood. we'll walk through the Optimize console + a couple models of expected costs and then dive into a few what-if scenarios, sound good?
[00:00:25] Anika: Yeah that's perfect. we're primarily concerned with 200ms p95 targets and cost for ~10M monthly tokens, FYI.
[00:00:33] Samir: Great, that's helpful. quick qual: are these mostly short assistant-style turns with a shared session context? or longer doc summarization calls?
[00:00:42] Priya: Mostly assistant chat, 8-12 tokens per user utterance on average, and then a 120-300 token model response. we do some retrieval-augmented prompts so prefix length varies.
[00:00:53] Jules: OK, got it. that distribution makes batching and KV prefix hits pretty valuable. i'll start with the baseline cost table we use in the console — assumptions are in the sheet: $0.00003 per input token, $0.00006 per output token for the model family we're simulating — these are example hosted numbers, dedicated reduces unit cost by ~20-35% depending on commit.
[00:01:14] Ralph: can you remind me how the batching multiplier works? we've tried naive batching but saw worse tail latency.
[00:01:21] Jules: sure — so continuous batching in Redwood tries to group concurrent requests into one kernel run. multiplier is basically how many tokens you amortize across a single forward. for example at 16 concurrent small-turn requests you might get a 6–8x token amortization versus single-request. however that only helps if the latency budget allows a small queueing delay and your concurrency distribution supports it.
[00:01:45] Priya: what about P99, does batching hurt P99 badly?
[00:01:49] Jules: it can if you rely solely on batching and have a wide arrival distribution. that's why we recommend mixed strategies: keep a small concurrency window for low-latency tails (session-affinity or fast-path lane) and a batching lane for bulk throughput. Also, prefix/KV cache reduces total forward work if the KV hit is high.
[00:02:07] [00:02:07] Diego (interrupts): Quick question — the 'KV cache' you mention, is that per-session or shared? we have multi-tenant constraints.
[00:02:13] Samir: good question. the cache is per-model instance but can be session-keyed; in hosted it's logically isolated per customer. for private we can run within your VPC too. there are RBAC + KMS controls so you can keep key material inside your HSM.
[00:02:29] Priya: i heard 'per-model instance' but can we tune TTLs? some of our sessions are long-running.
[00:02:34] Jules: yes TTLs and eviction policies are configurable. also prefetch lookahead: if you can predict the next top-k prompts or retrieval chunks, we can precompute KV entries and warm the cache which pushes hit rates up significantly.
[00:02:47] [00:02:47] Anika: do you have any numbers for hit-rate vs cost? like 30% hit vs 70% vs 90%?
[00:02:53] Jules: yep — on slide 3 of the sheet i just shared (link in chat) we modeled three scenarios: low (25% hit), mid (55% hit), high (80% hit). with our baseline token costs and your distribution, for 10M tokens per month these map to approximate monthly inference spend: low ~ $1,900, mid ~ $1,200, high ~ $700 — again hosted numbers. dedicated commitments drop these by roughly 25% on it.
[00:03:19] Ralph: that's a big delta, what's the realistic effort to move from 25% to 55%?
[00:03:24] Jules: usually a combination of short-term and medium-term work. short-term: add a simple prefix hashing and session affinity so identical initial prompts hit the KV. medium-term: lookahead prefetch and retrieval alignment, plus small prompt engineering to normalize tokens. in many producers we see a 20–30 point improvement within a couple weeks of engineering work.
[00:03:41] Priya: what about the cost of prefetching? isn't prefetching more ops?
[00:03:45] Jules: prefetching does consume compute, but it's usually cheaper than full model forward because you can precompute smaller prefix KV states and those are lightweight. the net depends on your prediction precision; our cost model factors in false-positive prefetch rates — if your prefetch precision is low it can backfire, which we call prefetch leakage in the sheet.
[00:04:03] [00:04:03] Diego: i think our SRE will want specific latencies under a VPC deployment — any differences we should expect between hosted and private?
[00:04:10] Samir: network hop differences are the main thing. hosted runs in our infra so you get our optimized kernel selections and autoscaling. private (VPC) adds network latency and some variability depending on your on-prem network; however you gain control over data residency and audit logs. dedicated in our cloud is often a sweet spot for latency + predictable unit cost.
[00:04:29] Anika: can you show the Console where batching rules are declared?
[00:04:33] Jules: yeah i'll share screen —
[00:04:36] [00:04:36] (screen share) Jules: here is the Optimize console -> Simulations tab. you can tune batch size caps, max wait ms, and a routing policy. path A is 'latency-first' (max wait 15ms, small batch cap 4), path B 'throughput' (max wait 60ms, batch cap 32). you can assign traffic weights.
[00:04:57] Priya: what's the effect on throughput when we go from cap 4 to cap 32?
[00:05:01] Jules: in our sim, cap 4 yields about 1.4x throughput improvement over no batching because of kernel amortization; cap 32 yields 6–9x depending on model sequence length. again, real numbers depend on your request mix.
[00:05:12] [00:05:12] Ralph: can we pick per-route policies? we have different SLAs for chat vs background classification.
[00:05:16] Jules: yes, per-route and per-model. for chat you'd pick latency-first and maybe prefix caching, for classification you can route to throughput lane.
[00:05:23] Priya: show me the simulation for our 200ms p95 target please.
[00:05:26] Jules: pulling up custom sim — based on your distribution and a 200ms p95 target, the recommended config is: latency lane (20% traffic) max wait 12ms batch cap 6, throughput lane (80%) max wait 50ms batch cap 20, KV TTL 30 minutes, prefetch precision target 0.6. that sim estimates a p95 of ~180ms and monthly cost ~ $1,050 under mid-hit assumptions.
[00:05:50] [00:05:50] Anika: cool, how sensitive is that to concurrency spikes?
[00:05:54] Jules: very sensitive. if concurrency doubles suddenly, the batching lane helps but tail latency may increase unless you autoscale faster. we recommend burst capacity and a canary fallback route (lower-cost smaller model) if the queue depth exceeds thresholds.
[00:06:10] Samir: i'll note here — Redwood Dedicated offers predictable queue depths and reserved GPUs which smooth out that variability; hosted can still do it but needs autoscale headroom.
[00:06:19] Ralph: any privacy/telemetry implications of prefix caching? we need auditability for tokens used in cache keys.
[00:06:26] Jules: prefix keys are hashed and auditable. we can enable token redaction in logs and keep only non-sensitive hashes. for compliance we have SOC2 docs and can do per-customer KMS in Private. link is in chat.
[00:06:41] [00:06:41] Priya: earlier you mentioned small forward work for KV hits — can you clarify what 'small' means?
[00:06:46] Jules: sure — when the KV is hit you skip the full decoder stack for the prefix tokens and only decode the new suffix. it's ~25–40% of full compute for many architectures depending on prefix length. imperfect transcription sometimes calls it 'K V cash' haha.
[00:07:02] [00:07:02] Diego: for the sandbox run, what do you need from us?
[00:07:06] Jules: sample traffic trace (JSON or CSV) with timestamps and full prompts, a small curated corpus for retrieval alignment, and a target SLA matrix — you've already given the 200ms p95. Priya, could you share the trace?
[00:07:18] Priya: yes i'll export and send it.
[00:07:21] Samir: great. next i'll go over the pricing sheet assumptions quickly —
[00:07:25] [00:07:25] (Samir shares link) Samir: baseline per-token math is here: we assume 10M output tokens, average output length 160 tokens per session, x price. the sheet has toggles for KV hit and batching multipliers so you can see cost curves.
[00:07:40] Ralph: do you model the cost of cold cache misses for new users?
[00:07:44] Jules: yes we include cold miss penalty and warm-up transient. the first 10% of sessions typically have lower hit rates which we call the ramp. the sim includes a 30-day warmup schedule.
[00:07:55] [00:07:55] Anika: how do we decide between dedicated vs hosted vs private for our profile?
[00:07:59] Jules: short answer: hosted if you want fastest time to market; dedicated if you need predictable throughput and committed discounts; private if you need strict network controls and on-prem compliance. for Stellarium with aggressive p95 and 10M tokens, dedicated looks attractive if you're willing to commit 3–6 months.
[00:08:16] [00:08:16] Priya: i want to understand the unit economics for quantized / 8-bit models — any difference in the sim?
[00:08:21] Jules: yes quantization reduces per-token compute cost and token pricing in the sheet has an optional quantized model line. that typically reduces inference spend by another 10–30% but can change latency characteristics slightly.
[00:08:34] Ralph: can we run a quick what-if: 80% KV hit and batch cap 24, what does p95 look like?
[00:08:41] Jules: quick eyeball: that pushes p95 under 150ms and monthly cost under $700 — i'll validate with the exact sim and put the run in the sandbox.
[00:08:52] [00:08:52] Diego: our infra folks will ask about telemetry hooks and token-level chargebacks. do you have token-level traces?
[00:08:58] Samir: yes per-token breakdown is available in Console — cost by route, by model, and a token-level histogram you can export.
[00:09:06] Anika: any notable tradeoffs with using smaller context windows to boost batching?
[00:09:10] Jules: reducing context reduces per-request compute but may reduce quality; prefix caching helps so you can keep context but avoid recomputing same prefixes. another approach is dynamic truncation combined with retrieval to maintain quality.
[00:09:24] [00:09:24] (10 minute mark)
[00:09:25] Samir: ok let's speed through the rest: i'll summarize recommended three-step plan for you: 1) pilot sandbox w/ 2-week load tests to measure real hit rates, 2) implement session affinity + prefix normalization to raise KV hits, 3) evaluate dedicated commit if sustained throughput looks economical.
[00:09:43] Ralph: timeline wise we could try the sandbox in two weeks.
[00:09:46] Priya: yes that works. i'll allocate eng time to share traces.
[00:09:50] Jules: perfect. i'll prepare the load test harness and a config template for the batching lanes.
[00:09:56] [00:09:56] Anika: any other security docs we need? we already asked for SOC2 + network diagram.
[00:10:01] Samir: we'll send SOC2 and a network diagram link to the VPC guide — Samir will attach certs in the follow-up email.
[00:10:08] [00:10:08] (longer technical Qs follow — excerpts)
[00:10:10] Priya: does the KV store support partial KV matches? like fuzzy prefix equivalence?
[00:10:14] Jules: we support deterministic prefix hashing and approximate fuzzy lookup via embedding-based keys in the Optimize pipelines. costs are higher for the fuzzy path but it improves hit-rate for paraphrases.
[00:10:26] Diego: what's the fallback model architecture you recommend for canaries?
[00:10:29] Jules: a smaller 8-bit quantized variant of the same family works well; same tokenizer keeps prompts aligned.
[00:10:35] Priya: ok. one last quick thing — can the console emit an exportable CSV of simulation scenarios for our finance folks?
[00:10:41] Jules: yep there's an Export CSV button under each sim. we'll include an exported baseline and the high-hit scenario in the follow-up.
[00:10:49] [00:10:49] (wrap-up)
[00:10:50] Samir: to recap next steps: we'll send the cost sheet, SOC2 + network diagrams, schedule the sandbox run, Jules will prepare load test plan. Priya will send traffic traces.
[00:11:02] Priya: noted.
[00:11:04] Ralph: thanks, that's helpful.
[00:11:06] Samir: great thanks everyone, we'll follow up by email with links and a proposed sandbox slot.
[00:11:13] Anika: thanks all.
